questions.subject: Physics
questions.learningObjective: Use wave quantities to interpret observations and distinguish changes in speed, frequency and wavelength.
questions.prompt: A buoy completes 18 oscillations in 12 s. Crests are 2.4 m apart. Calculate the wave frequency and speed.

markingGuide.description: Divide 18 oscillations by 12 s to obtain 1.5 Hz.

questions.explanation: Divide 18 oscillations by 12 s to obtain 1.5 Hz. Use speed = frequency × wavelength. Give 3.6 m/s.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.learningObjective: Use wave quantities to interpret observations and distinguish changes in speed, frequency and wavelength.
questions.prompt: At one instant the first and fifth crests on a rope are 3.2 m apart. A marked point on the rope reaches a crest every 0.4 s. Find the wavelength and period, and explain why five crests do not represent five wavelengths.
questions.answer: Wavelength 0.8 m, period 0.4 s. Five successive crests bound four crest-to-crest intervals.

markingGuide.description: Divide 3.2 m by four to get 0.8 m.

questions.explanation: Identify four intervals. Divide 3.2 m by four to get 0.8 m. Identify the period as 0.4 s.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.learningObjective: Use wave quantities to interpret observations and distinguish changes in speed, frequency and wavelength.
questions.prompt: A ripple travels from deep water into shallow water, where its speed is lower. The same source continues vibrating at a steady rate. Predict the changes in frequency and wavelength, and explain.
questions.answer: Frequency stays fixed by the source. Wavelength decreases because speed decreases at the same frequency.

markingGuide.description: Explain that the source still sends the same number of crests per second.
Use wavelength = speed ÷ frequency to infer a shorter wavelength.

questions.explanation: State that frequency remains unchanged. Explain that the source still sends the same number of crests per second. Use wavelength = speed ÷ frequency to infer a shorter wavelength.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.learningObjective: Use wave quantities to interpret observations and distinguish changes in speed, frequency and wavelength.
questions.prompt: Which measurement gives the amplitude of a transverse wave on a rope?
questions.answer: The greatest displacement of a point on the rope from its rest position
options: The distance between successive crests
The greatest displacement of a point on the rope from its rest position
The time between successive crests at a marker
The distance a crest travels in one second
questions.explanation: Amplitude measures displacement from equilibrium, not spacing or speed.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.learningObjective: Use wave quantities to interpret observations and distinguish changes in speed, frequency and wavelength.
questions.prompt: A rope wave travels to the right. A coloured knot tied to the rope moves repeatedly up and down. What does the observation illustrate?
questions.answer: The medium oscillates perpendicular to the direction of propagation.
options: The medium oscillates perpendicular to the direction of propagation.
Each knot travels to the right with the crest.
The rope carries matter steadily to the right.
The wave is longitudinal because the knot moves.
questions.explanation: Transverse displacement is perpendicular to the direction in which the disturbance travels.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.learningObjective: Use wave quantities to interpret observations and distinguish changes in speed, frequency and wavelength.
questions.prompt: The rate of vibration of a sound source doubles. The sound still travels in the same air at unchanged conditions. What happens to its wavelength?
options: It doubles.
It stays unchanged.
It becomes four times as large.
It halves.
questions.explanation: With speed fixed, wavelength is inversely proportional to frequency.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.learningObjective: Explain wave behaviour at boundaries and openings and interpret echo travel times.
questions.prompt: A pulse is sent straight towards a cliff. The echo returns 0.70 s later. If the speed of sound is 340 m/s, calculate the distance to the cliff.

markingGuide.description: Recognise that the time covers the outward and return paths.

questions.explanation: Recognise that the time covers the outward and return paths. Calculate 340 × 0.70 ÷ 2. Give 119 m.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.learningObjective: Explain wave behaviour at boundaries and openings and interpret echo travel times.
questions.prompt: A pupil says sound heard around a corner proves that air is flowing around the corner from the speaker to the listener. Evaluate the claim using wave behaviour.
questions.answer: The observation can be explained by diffraction as sound spreads around an edge. The disturbance transfers energy without a sustained flow of air from the speaker to the listener.

markingGuide.description: Identify diffraction around an edge as a plausible explanation.
Distinguish local particle oscillation from bulk air movement.

questions.explanation: Identify diffraction around an edge as a plausible explanation. Distinguish local particle oscillation from bulk air movement.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.learningObjective: Explain wave behaviour at boundaries and openings and interpret echo travel times.
questions.prompt: A light ray enters glass from air along the normal. Its speed decreases. Explain why its direction stays the same and state what happens to its wavelength.
questions.answer: At normal incidence the angle to the normal is zero, so the transmitted ray continues straight. Frequency stays fixed and the lower speed means a shorter wavelength.

markingGuide.description: Identify zero incidence and zero refraction angles.
Link the reduced speed to a reduced wavelength.

questions.explanation: Identify zero incidence and zero refraction angles. State that frequency remains unchanged. Link the reduced speed to a reduced wavelength.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.learningObjective: Explain wave behaviour at boundaries and openings and interpret echo travel times.
questions.prompt: Two water waves of different wavelengths reach identical openings. One wavelength is close to the opening width and the other is much smaller. Which spreads more noticeably beyond its opening?
questions.answer: The wave whose wavelength is close to the opening width
options: The wave whose wavelength is close to the opening width
The wave whose wavelength is much smaller
Both always spread by the same amount
Neither wave can spread beyond an opening
questions.explanation: Diffraction is more pronounced when the opening is comparable with the wavelength.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.learningObjective: Explain wave behaviour at boundaries and openings and interpret echo travel times.
questions.prompt: A ray passes from air into a transparent liquid at an oblique angle. Its speed in the liquid is lower. How does the refracted ray bend?
options: Away from the normal
Through a right angle in all cases
Back into the air as the transmitted ray
Towards the normal
questions.explanation: At oblique incidence, entering a medium of lower wave speed reduces the angle to the normal.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.learningObjective: Explain wave behaviour at boundaries and openings and interpret echo travel times.
questions.prompt: A student wants to use an echo to measure the distance to a wall. Which measurement would most directly reduce uncertainty due to background noise?
questions.answer: Repeat the pulse several times and compare the delays of the distinct returning echoes.
options: Time the first unrelated sound heard after each pulse.
Use the loudness of the outgoing pulse as the elapsed time.
Repeat the pulse several times and compare the delays of the distinct returning echoes.
Add the delay from a different wall to the measured delay.
questions.explanation: Repeated measurements of identifiable echoes help distinguish a consistent delay from unrelated noise.
